Meccan, and its verses are 3. "It was revealed after Al-Sharh."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

He swears by the Asr prayer, because of its excellence, as evidenced by the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the middle prayer﴾ (al-Salat al-Wusta), which is the Asr prayer, as it is in the codex of Hafsah. And the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever misses the Asr prayer, it is as if he has lost his family and his wealth." [Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.] And because the obligation to perform it is more burdensome, since people are busy with their trades and earnings at the end of the day, and occupied with their livelihoods.

Or He swears by the evening, just as He swears by the forenoon, because both contain signs of divine power. Or He swears by time, because in its passing there are all kinds of wonders.

"Man" is used generically for the human species. "Loss" (al-khusr) means ruin (al-khusran), as it has been said: "Disbelief is in ingratitude (al-kufr fi al-kufran)." The meaning is: people are in loss in their trade, except for the righteous alone, because they bought the Hereafter with the world, so they profited and were made happy; and as for everyone else, they traded contrary to their trade, so they fell into ruin and wretchedness.

﴿And they enjoin one another to the truth﴾: to the established matter which cannot be lawfully denied, and that is all good: the affirmation of Allah's oneness and obedience to Him, following His books and messengers, detachment from the world, and desire for the Hereafter. ﴿And they enjoin one another to patience﴾: patience in refraining from sins and in persisting in acts of obedience, and patience over what Allah tries His servants with.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the Surah 'Wal-Asr', Allah will forgive him, and he will be among those who enjoin one another to the truth and enjoin one another to patience." [Narrated by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, and Ibn Mardawayh, with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
